<meta>This page is the editor's preface to the 1722 edition of the *Aurea Catena Homeri* (The Golden Chain of Homer). It follows the title page and a short philosophical epigraph. The editor is justifying the publication of what was previously a secret, expensive manuscript.</meta>

## First Preliminary Note of the Editor.

To the kind reader, I hereby present a Physical and Chemical little work <note>German: *Wercklein*; the editor uses a humble diminutive, though he immediately stresses its great value.</note> of great worth, the likes of which has likely hardly ever come before his eyes. It is reliably reported that this manuscript was previously paid for with as much as a thousand <term>Thalers</term> <note>A silver coin used throughout Europe; a thousand Thalers would have been a small fortune, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a master craftsman.</note>; indeed, even recently and up to this time, many have given 30, 40, 50, 60, and up to 100 Thalers for its communication. A foreign lover of chemistry wrote the following to me regarding this on June 27th of this year, 1722, after I had sent him a copy out of special friendship:

> “The **method of sweetening** <note>Latin: *Methodum dulcificandi*; in alchemy, this refers to removing corrosive acids or salts from a substance to make it medicinal.</note> and **volatilizing fixed alkalis** <note>German/Latin: *alcalia fixa zu volatilisiren*; the process of turning stable, heat-resistant salts into a vaporous or 'spiritual' state.</note> I practiced nine years ago, and thereby, **by means of a third agent** <note>Latin: *per tertium*; referring to a third substance used to bridge or react two others.</note>, performed extraordinary and miraculous cures for **cancer**, **gangrene**, **stones** <note>Latin: *Calculo*; likely kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and **pleurisy** <note>Latin: *Pleuritide*; an inflammation of the lungs.</note>. Twelve years ago, I would have gladly paid a thousand **florins** <note>Germanized Latin: *florenen*; another common gold or silver currency.</note> for such a manuscript. Now, it is a pleasure to see that others have traveled the same path and discovered the same **from practice** <note>Latin: *ex praxi*.</note>.”

To be sure, various people who have this writing in their hands will be quite reluctant to see it now appear in print and be made public. However, since the intention of the author (who remains unknown to date) was certainly that it should benefit many through publication—as can be clearly seen here and there, but especially on page 320—and since it has also been copied by hand quite frequently in these years, leading to a strong suspicion that it would eventually be brought to light by one person or another: I hope they will not take this undertaking so much amiss, while others will be grateful that such a highly valuable thing is given to them for a small price out of good intentions

<meta>This page continues the editor's preface from the 1722 edition. Having previously mentioned the high cost and rarity of the manuscript, the editor now explains his editorial process. He describes merging three different versions of the text to provide the most complete edition possible for the reader, while maintaining the author's original, unpolished style.</meta>

### First Preliminary Note.

...is hereby communicated, and indeed in the most faithful and complete manner possible, as the work was still obtainable at the time. For after three different copies <term>Exemplaria</term> <note>Latin: manuscript copies.</note> from different locations came into my hands, I diligently compared <term>collated</term> <note>Latin: *conferiret*; the scholarly process of comparing different versions of a text to find the most accurate reading.</note> them with the help of a good friend; and since one contained a good deal more than the others, the deficiency found in most copies has been remedied here. 

Meanwhile, I did not wish to change anything arbitrarily, nor correct that which may have been previously overlooked in copying or misread; rather, I have intentionally left everything as I found it, only that here and there in parentheses <term>parenthesi</term> it has been noted where there was a variant reading <term>varians lectio</term> <note>Latin: a different wording or spelling found in a different manuscript copy.</note>. If here and there the author's Latin did not turn out well, etc., one can easily forgive him, especially when considering how he describes himself on page 162. And what does the reader care for elegant words and style <term>Stylo</term>? It is enough if the presentation is otherwise clear, and more profound knowledge can be drawn from it than I am able to extol with many words in this narrow space. 

Regarding the title of the book, we wished to avoid all charlatanry and preferred to set it simply as the author himself drafted it. One might well have added a third part regarding the transmutation of metals <term>de Transmutatione Metallorum</term> <note>Latin: the alchemical transformation of base metals into gold or silver.</note>, which the owners <term>Possessores</term> <note>Referring to the previous private owners of the secret manuscripts.</note> wish to attribute to our writer and which they value <term>æstimiren</term> very highly; he himself also makes some mention of such things on page 243. However, we have hesitated to do so for the time being. What may yet happen in this regard in the future, we shall leave to time. In the meantime, let the kind reader use these two parts for the glory of **God**, for toward Him all knowledge <term>Erkäntniß</term> <note>German: *Erkenntnis*; deeper spiritual or scientific insight into the workings of the world.</note> even in nature should lead us; and fare well!

# Explanation of the Figure
## of the *Double Abyss* <note>Latin: *Abyssi Duplicatæ*</note>,
### or
## Of the doubly volatile and fixed abyss.

One abyss calls out to the other,
Together they engage in a hard struggle:
The volatile should become entirely fixed,
Vapor and water turn themselves into earth.
Heaven itself must be earthly,
Otherwise no life enters into the soil.
The uppermost should be the lowermost,
The lowermost should again be the uppermost.
The fixed shall become entirely volatile,
The earth should be a water and vapor,
The earth must fly up highest to heaven,
Heaven must crawl into the center of the earth.
Thus heaven and earth must be inverted,
Should the lowermost become the uppermost.
The volatile <term>Dragon</term> <note>In alchemy, the "Dragon" is a common symbol for matter. The "volatile" dragon usually represents mercury or spirit, while the "fixed" dragon represents the solid body or salt.</note> kills the more fixed one,
The fixed one compels the volatile one to death.
Thus must clearly come to light
The <term>Quintessence</term> <note>Literally the "fifth essence"; the purest, most concentrated medicinal or spiritual force extracted from a substance.</note> and what it is capable of.

# The Golden Chain of Homer

When he becomes fixed and flashes no more,
And his Eve sits by his side.
The Sun and Moon, the sea and earth
Turn him toward Eve through constant motion.
Through heat and cold, through the sea's steady course,
Eve rises up with Adam,
<note>Adam and Eve are used here as alchemical metaphors for the masculine/active and feminine/passive principles, often associated with Sulfur and Mercury.</note>
⊝ Who is commonly called Salt and Alkali,
Feeding all the world's children with her blood:
For when man and woman step together,
A perfect fruit is forged.
⊕ The Acid and the alkaline salt
Provide the fat for every soup. <note>A metaphorical way of saying these elements provide the essential substance or "richness" of the matter.</note>
⊖ The volatile kingdom of animals testifies to such,
Neither volatile nor fixed—mark that well.
⨁ The vegetable hermaphrodite
Also shows from what it was forged. <note>The "hermaphrodite" refers to the alchemical Rebis, a single body containing both male and female properties.</note>
🜔 The fixed ores and stones testify,
That they belong to <term>Niter</term> <note>Potassium nitrate or saltpeter, viewed by alchemists as a universal celestial salt.</note> and Salt.
Fire and air, water and earth
Desire the active part of him.
🜛 Now when the noble World-Seed is made fixed,
And steam and water are brought to earth,
Then it is made and also accomplished,
That which all the world holds in highest esteem.
The volatile must become the fixed,
Turning from water and steam toward the earth,
And when it becomes a red, dry blood,
Then it is the world's treasure and highest good.
♀ A complete perfection,
Which drives away all poverty and sickness.

## Preface.

A highly-inclined artist and lover <note>The term "lover" here refers to a "lover of the arts" or an amateur enthusiast</note> should take note that this treatise proceeds quite simply, according to nature itself <note>original: "secundum ipsam naturam"</note> both theoretically and practically <note>original: "theoretice & practice"</note> throughout, with demonstrations and proofs everywhere of the fundamental, true causes and the reason <note>original: "Rationem"</note>—how? in what manner? and why? and from what this or that arises and becomes? And this is done because if such an artist does not know the way of nature, and does not know how nature works, he cannot possibly understand the art; instead, he must fall blindly upon the prescribed processes, working through them and failing in them many times over, because he understands neither the reason <note>original: "rationem"</note> nor the rule of nature <note>original: "regulam Naturæ"</note>. For these reasons, many thousands have run the path of their temporal ruin, and likely many have even run toward eternal ruin out of desperation.

But from the present treatise, he shall

<summary>The author introduces the preface by emphasizing that the treatise follows the laws of nature both theoretically and practically to prevent artists from falling into ruin through blind experimentation.</summary>

# Preface

the most beautiful and simplest order of nature, and to have a regulated guiding principle, which will—not improperly—point him toward the path of all birth and destruction of natural things as clearly as one teaches children the A.B.C.s, and will explain everywhere why this or that happens, how, in what manner, and to what end such things occur.

Lest I linger too long in a very extensive description of natural things—since various authors have already sufficiently and superfluously embellished and decorated such matters with entire folio volumes—I shall proceed quite briefly and with little mention of unnecessary things, thereby avoiding an excess of paper and, above all, the annoyance of the reader.

It is also to be noted that no ornament of eloquence or strained style is to be sought here, as I myself *walk simply and plainly, according to the simplicity of Nature herself, with bare feet* <note>original: "simplex simpliciter secundum ipsius Naturæ simplicitatem nudo pede incedire." The author emphasizes a rejection of academic pretension in favor of natural truth.</note>. It is of no use to an artist <note>term: Artist (Artisten). # Preface.

...make it effective, visible, and tangible through **practical application** <note>original: "Praxi practicata"</note>. Otherwise, if it remains stuck only in a theoretical mind, he may call himself a debater, but not a practitioner.

Now, he who undertakes to contemplate the essence of all natural things—their birth, life, and death—should and must carefully consider the origin of Nature from beginning to end. That is, how and from what Nature gives birth to, sustains, and again destroys the things contained here in the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, and each of them in particular: such as the **universal phenomena** <note>original: "Meteora universalia," referring to atmospheric and celestial events</note>, animals, herbs, and ores. He must observe how Nature herself dissolves, congeals, re-resolves, and regenerates them. For whatever Nature makes, and through whatever means she makes it, she destroys everything again through those very same means. Thus, every single thing carries its own **congealer** <note>original: "Coagulatorem"</note> and **dissolver** <note>original: "Resolutorem"</note> with it—its life and death upon its own back. By one thing it is born and sustained, and by that very same thing it is again broken and destroyed. For according to the distinction of the operations and the **methods of operation** <note>original: "modi operationis"</note>, a different action and effect results.

# The First Book
## The First Part.
# ON THE GENERATION OF THINGS. <note>original: "DE GENERATIONE RERVM"</note>
## Concerning the Procreation and Birth of Natural Things.

---

### The First Chapter.
### What Nature Is.

Nature is the mass of the visible and present world gathered together by the Creator, with all its inherent visible and invisible creatures—whatever works its essence in this world, aside from God alone. Although some, for the better understanding of mankind, have divided this world into the natural-visible and the supernatural-invisible, none of this concerns us here; for we believe that each and every thing was made naturally by God out of the <term>Chaos</term> <note>In early modern alchemy and philosophy, "Chaos" refers to the primordial, unformed matter from which God created the universe.</note> and the great Nothingness.

## The II. Chapter.

### From whom or out of what everything was born, and how it originated.

The incomprehensible GOD created everything out of His arbitrary will from the great Nothingness. For He resolved and willed, and let go forth from His Divine Mouth His holy, powerful word *Fiat!* <note>Latin: "Let it be done!"</note> which became an immeasurable vapor, mist, and smoke. This vapor, etc., resolved or condensed <note>original: "resolvirte oder condensirte [al. concentrirte]"—the author suggests the vapor either settled or concentrated its essence</note> and thickened itself through its ever-following <note>alternative reading: "everlasting"</note> increase into the universally known Chaotic Water. This water now is that from which this great world with all its inhabitants was made; and this water is that from which GOD made all supernatural and natural things; and this water is the primordial or original source of all things that shall come before and after us.

The origin, however, of such water is, as taught, the eternal GOD and His released Word; the Word is a Spirit full of power, and this Spirit became visible as a vapor and mist, and this became tangible as a water.

Here we have now two things enclosed in one: a visible thing, which is water, and an invisible thing, which is the Spirit, that lies hidden within the water.

# Part 1, Chapter 3: How All Things Were Born

# Chapter IV.
## In what manner this Universal Seed was conceived and born.

After God divided the simple chaos <note>original: "chaos simplum"; the undifferentiated state of matter before creation</note> into four parts <note>original: "quadruplum"; the four elements</note>, he immediately imposed upon them the command: "increase and multiply" <note>original: "crescite & multiplicamini"; Genesis 1:22</note>.

The heaven and air are the father, the husband, the active <note>original: "Agens"</note> or working part; the water and earth are the mother, the wife, the passive <note>original: "Patiens"</note> or suffering part.

These four—and yet only two—must stand together and awaken a seed in the first matter <note>original: "prima materia"</note>, a regenerated chaotic water or primordial chaos, out of their innermost being or center. This is for the birth, preservation, destruction, and rebirth of all things, until such time as God melts the mass of the great world together into a single stone.

The number of those who are meant to forge this seed or regenerated chaos, the Spirit of the World <note>original: "Spiritum mundi"; the vital essence permeating the universe</note>, consists of four, as has been said: Heaven or Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.

However, although these four appear entirely contrary to one another when one extreme is viewed against the other, and in such a conflicting manner could never accomplish anything good; nevertheless, when they come together in an orderly fashion, they accomplish everything and anything that has been commanded of them by the Creator.

# Part 1, Chapter 4: In what manner the Universal—

For the philosophical axiom must indeed be and remain true, namely: *One cannot pass from one extreme to another extreme without a middle.* <note>original: "Non transiri posse ab uno extremo ad alterum extremum absque medio." This is a fundamental rule in alchemy: opposites cannot be joined directly; they require a bridge.</note> Every <term>Artist</term> <note>A practitioner of the alchemical arts.</note> should note this very well. For thousands upon thousands err and fail solely because they do not rightly consider or observe this point.

For the Heaven can never become Earth without the mediation of Water and Air; and the Earth can never become Heaven without Water and Air as the <term>middle-things</term> <note>Substances that share properties with both extremes, allowing them to bond.</note> between Heaven and Earth. Likewise, the Heaven can hardly become Water without Air, nor can the Earth become Air without the mediation of Water.

The Heaven is subtle, pure, clear, thin, and <term>volatile</term> <note>original: "flüchtig." Substances that evaporate or escape when heated.</note>; the Earth, <note>original: "e contra"</note> on the contrary, is coarse, thick, dark, and highly <term>fixed</term>. <note>original: "fix." Substances that resist the fire and do not evaporate.</note> These two are contrary <note>original: "ex tota sua proprietate"</note> in their entire property. For if one wished to bind and fix the Heaven (as the highest volatile) together with the Earth (as the highest fixed), he would never be able to do it: for the highest volatile flees away into its <term>Chaos</term> <note>The primordial state of unformed matter or the atmosphere.</note> at the slightest coming heat, and leaves the fixed behind. This happens in all things of the whole of Nature: that the highest volatile and the highest fixed can never be bound or united without their middle-thing. An Artist should have this before his eyes without ceasing, so that he does not lose matter, time, and expense.

Therefore, whoever wishes to turn the Heaven or Fire into Earth, let him first unite them with their middle; then they will unite <note>original: "in puncto momenti"</note> in a single moment, remaining stable in any fire, whereas before they would have required, so to speak, an eternal time for their union.

# Seed has been begotten and born.

Let the Heaven rise into Air as a medium; in this way, they unite immediately without conflict, because they are both of a subtle nature. When these are united, then give them Water as a medium between Air and Earth, and they will unite once again in a single point; then give them Earth. In this way, the union occurs by descending from the most subtle grade to the subtle, from this to the thick, and from there to the thicker <note>original: "descendendo à gradu subtilissimo ad subtilem, ab hoc ad crassum, inde ad crassiorem"</note>. It does not jump from the most subtle directly to the thickest, but achieves union through the appropriate intermediate steps.

The same applies in reverse: turn the Earth into Water by means of Water; turn this into Air through the Air; and transform this into Heaven with and through the Heaven. For they are one in their matter and origin; therefore, one must be the helper <insert>and guide</insert> of the other, and one must be prepared by means of the other.

This is how it must be, and this rule of Nature cannot be bypassed at all; rather, unite the Heaven with the Air, the Air with the Water, and the Water with the Earth. Or conversely: unite the Earth with the Water, the Water with the Air, and the Air with the Heaven or Fire. In this manner, the Heaven is turned into Earth and the Earth into Heaven. For the Heaven is very subtle, and the Air is also subtle, yet one degree coarser than the Heaven; likewise, the Water is one degree thicker and coarser than the Air, and the Earth is one degree thicker and coarser than the Water. Thus, one must proceed step-by-step in the most beautiful order of Nature itself: then a right, concentrated harmony and a true <term>quintessentialized operation</term> <note>An alchemical process aimed at extracting the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual core of a substance</note> arises. This is how it must be in all chemical opera-

But someone will object: Your <term>proposition<note>A formal statement or argument put forward for consideration.</note></term> does not quite fit here. For should the air be only one degree more subtle than the water, and the water only one degree more subtle than the earth? Since one sees that water is several degrees coarser than air, and thus the earth is many degrees coarser than water.

To satisfy this objection, the <term>Artist<note>In this context, the "Artist" refers to the alchemist or natural philosopher who works with the materials of nature.</note></term> must understand that just as the heavens as well as the air, water, and earth are divided into their <term>degrees of subtlety and thickness<note>original: "gradus subtilitatis & crassitudinis"</note></term>, so also these four <term>elements<note>original: "Elementa"</note></term> are divided among themselves. For the coarsest earth does not immediately mix with thin water, nor the coarsest water with the most subtle air, or the thickest air with the subtle heavens—no! # Seed has been begotten and born.

The Sphere <note>original: "Sphæra"; likely referring to the celestial influence or the cosmic structure</note>—no, rather it is Nature that has mixed the thick and thin earth together, indeed, forcing water and air, and even fire, into the mixture.

But here, in the anatomy <note>In this context, "anatomy" refers to the alchemical process of "cutting open" or analyzing a substance to see its internal components</note>, one first sees how the subtle rises up from the coarse and allows itself to be separated from it <insert>or: it separates itself</insert>. Nature, in her operation, is very beautifully regulated in a mixed fashion <note>original: "promiscue"</note>, so that she does not simply mix <note>original: "permisciret"</note> and throw one thing together with another, but rather one subtle part after another, as for example:

Take an earth from the field or meadow, whichever you wish; pour water upon it and stir it well together, so that the water and the earth are entirely mixed. Then let it stand for a while, and you will see that the water lets the coarse earth fall and only draws out the subtle, namely the salt; this unites itself immediately with the water as a virgin earth <note>A term for pure, unadulterated mineral matter that has not yet been "worked" by artifice</note>. But when this earth is out, the water will no longer attack the other coarse earth because it is too weak. Therefore, you must first turn the virgin earth, with and through the water, into a water itself—that is, distill it into a spiritual water. For then this water has the power once again to separate the remaining more subtle earths from the coarser ones and to make them like itself, so that they also become water; and this in turn attacks the remaining earth. In this manner, Nature works both by dissolving <note>original: "resolvendo"</note> and by coagulating <note>original: "coagulando"</note> in all things.

# Part I, Chapter 7: Concerning the Air

The heavens refine [matter] and convert it into its own nature, so that one is transformed into the other, now fixed, now volatile, with unceasing alternation. There, the extraction of the entire universe comes together, where the ancient Chaos—which was separated for so many ages and years—is daily and hourly conceived and regenerated anew, for the birth, preservation, destruction, and rebirth of all natural things.

This movement causes a lukewarmness; the lukewarmness causes a warming; the warming causes a heating. This heating excites and awakens the water into vapors and mists; and the stronger the heat and the more water there is, the more violently it steams, seethes, and vapors. 

When this vapor breaks out into the air, it is moved even more by the surrounding warmth of the air and the sun, and by the wind. The more it is moved, the more subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" means refined, purified, or becoming less physically dense.</note> it becomes, so that the longer it rises, the higher it goes; and the higher it rises, the closer it comes to the heavens; and the closer it comes to the heavens, the closer it comes to the origin of movement. This then causes this vapor, the longer it lasts, to be increasingly refined and made volatile until it reaches the highest degree. The more volatile it is made, however, the more it inclines toward the nature of the heavens, until it is changed by the heavens into a heavenly nature <gloss>alternatively: toward the nature of the heavens</gloss>, as was said above: just as the heavens, the closer they come to the earth, the more earthly they become, until they are converted by the earth into soil and stone.

Now it has been explained how this vapor is changed into air and heaven. Now we wish to examine what kind of vapor this is, and what it contains within itself.

# On the Regenerated Chaos and the Three Kingdoms

From the decayed seed or the **regenerated chaos** <note>The "chaos" refers to the primal, unformed matter from which alchemists believed all things originated.</note> and so forth, sub-lunary subjects are born. Indeed, if you wish, you can make the entire earth mineral in nature. Through this process of moistening and drying, you will find that the earth becomes heavy and sandy. 

**Note Well:** <note>original: "NB." (Nota Bene)</note> The flask must always be closed only with a paper stopper, and not sealed tightly, so that the air can also enter therein.

When you have a great deal of such sand, take some of it and perform an **assay** <note>original: "Probe"</note> just as one **tests ores** <note>original: "Erze probiret"</note>, and you will find a trace of silver and gold.

# Part 1, Chapter 10: Discovery of the True Universal

It is immediately said: "Yes, it is unfathomable to human understanding; God must always perform a <term>miracle</term> <note>original: "Miracul"</note> and reveal the <term>subject</term> <note>the base material or substance being worked upon</note> in a dream or through an <term>Adept</term> <note>a master who has attained the secret of the Philosopher's Stone</note>." Yet, it is often merely the <term>laborant's</term> <note>a practical chemist or assistant</note> own lack of understanding, because he pays no attention to what he has in his hands, what he is doing, or what effect it has produced. He does not examine the circumstances; he seeks no further advantage through reflection upon an accidental discovery. He does not ask: "If this produced that result, how? If I now added this to it, or took that away, what might come of it?" Instead, he lets everything pass by superficially, even though he should have this proverb in his head: **it is easy to add to things already invented** <note>original Latin: "inventis facile est addere"</note>.

Suppose an unlearned mason sees a house being built; he builds the house according to his simple concept, and once he has finished building it, he sees over time several inconvenient spots and defects in it. From this he immediately reasons: "Look, if I had done it this way, it would be more convenient; here I should have walled in an iron bar, then it would be stronger; or here wood, or a large durable stone; or here I should have built a squared room, high or low," etc. Now, if he no longer wanted to keep this house, sold it, and built himself another, he would already have ten advantages in correcting the previous mistakes. 

A laborant and <term>chemist</term> <note>original: "Chymicus"</note> should do exactly the same: when he has committed an error, he should examine it well—what was too much or too little, what effect this produced, what hindrance or advancement that piece provided, etc. He should inquire into the nature and property of every <term>subject</term> beforehand, so that he does not bring contrary things together.

# Chapter XV.

### That Nitre and Salt are to be found in minerals, and that minerals are made from these two, and can be resolved back into them.

The closer the Heavens approach the Earth, the more earthly and corporeal they become; and the more earthly they become, the more fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a substance that is stable under heat and does not evaporate.</note> they become; the more fixed they become, the less they burn, shine, or ignite. Thus is the Nitre <note>original: "Nitrum"; here referring to a volatile aerial spirit or saltpeter, believed to be a celestial life-force.</note> which has descended from the Heavens: it is entirely volatile and hidden invisibly within the water, but through putrefaction <note>The process of breaking down or fermenting a substance to release its inner essence.</note> it becomes manifest. The more earthly and fixed this Nitre becomes, the more alkaline <note>original: "alcalisch"</note> it becomes, and through such fixation it loses more and more of its lightning-bolt <note>original: "Fulmen"; the explosive, energetic quality of the celestial spirit.</note>, as can be seen here with the minerals. For the more it steps out of its universal nature, the more it changes its nature; thus it acquires one nature and quality when it specifies itself into the Animal Kingdom, another in the Vegetable Kingdom, and yet another in the Mineral Kingdom. However, it proves its fiery dominion in all of these, to a greater or lesser degree, according to how fixed or volatile it is in its grade: in the animal and vegetable kingdoms, it resides in the coarse and subtle oiliness, resin, pitch, and gums; in the mineral kingdom, it resides in sulfurous things, such as Sulfur, Naphtha, Petroleum, etc.

## The XVI. Chapter.
### Concerning the Main Portal and Key of Nature, as the Author of all Birth and Destruction of Natural Things: Putrefaction.

The heavens, because of their divisibility <note>original: "Zertheilheit," likely meaning refined or ethereal composition</note> [or delicacy] and subtle purity, are not as changeable as the lower elements; however, when the heavens descend into the air, and from there onto the water and earth, they rot along with the others in order to also give birth to their likeness in the lower elements. Without putrefaction, by the special order of God, these elements will neither give birth to nor destroy anything.

Therefore, without putrefaction or preceding maceration <note>softening by soaking</note>, digestion, or fermentation (whether it happens quickly or slowly), no *Anatomia vera* <note>Latin: "True Anatomy." Here it refers to the true chemical analysis or separation of a substance's parts.</note> can be hoped for, in universal matters as well as in specifics and individuals.

For dew, rain, snow, hail, and frost rot without distinction, and create a separation of the subtle from the coarse; the sign of this is when they give off a—though faint—rotten smell.

# and the Key of Nature, Putrefaction.

The **Animals** decay very easily, like the higher substances, and because of their copious volatile parts <note>alternative reading: "their copious, very volatile saltpeter"</note> they stink unbearably.

The **Vegetables** also decay easily because of their superfluous moisture <note>original: "humidi"</note>, yet not as quickly as the **Animals**, nor do they stink quite as badly as the aforementioned.

The **Minerals** decay, ferment, or seethe; yet they do not give off—at least most of them—such an evil odor as previously mentioned. However, if iron enters into maceration <note>the process of softening or breaking down a substance by soaking in liquid</note> and attains its homogeneous state <note>original: "Homogeneum"; referring to the metal reaching a uniform, purified consistency</note>, it stinks worse than a sewer, which we shall leave for its proper place.

From **Putrefaction** <note>the process of decay or rotting, viewed by alchemists as a necessary stage of transformation</note> we now derive this benefit and change: that **Minerals** become **Vegetables**, **Vegetables** become **Animals**, and these **vice versa** <note>conversely</note> become **Vegetables** and **Minerals** again. And thus nature goes around in a ring, and makes the uppermost into the lowermost, and the lowermost into the uppermost. Indeed, she even converts all three kingdoms into a universal, indifferent nature, as we said above: she drives vapors from the **Center** of the earth- and water-sphere (as if from the kingdom of **Minerals**), and vapors **from the surface of the earth** <note>original: "ex superficie terræ"</note> (as if from the **vegetable kingdom**), and vapors from exhaling and decaying animals—as well as from the three living and flourishing kingdoms—into the air. There, she turns such things into chaos <note>original: "chaotisiret"; the process of returning matter to its primal, unformed state</note> and brings them to universality, which then must be and is neither animal, nor vegetable, nor mineral, but rather ubiquitous <note>original: "ubiquotistisch"; existing everywhere at once</note> and all in all.

Part 1. Chapter 17. What Putrefaction [is]

Few <term>adolescent philosophers<note>original: "Philosophi adolescentes"; likely referring to students or those new to the study of alchemy</note></term>, and even fewer of the common sort of <term>laboratory workers<note>original: "Laboranten"; those who perform chemical operations without understanding the underlying theory</note></term>, will believe such things before they are explained; however, after the explanation, every peasant sees it before his eyes at his very door, even before he steps outside, as we have partly discussed above.

Therefore, <term>putrefaction<note>original: "Putrefaction"; the process of rotting or decomposition, viewed by alchemists as a necessary stage of purification and rebirth</note></term> is that wonderful blacksmith who makes a water out of the earth, an air out of the water, the fire or the heavens out of the air; and out of the heavens it again makes air, from this water, and from the water earth. It brings about such changes without ceasing and without stopping at every minute of time, and continues until heaven and earth melt together into one glassy lump.

## The XVII. Chapter.
### What Putrefaction actually is.

When God released the <term>Universal Vapor<note>original: "Universal-Dampf"; the primordial substance or "First Matter" from which the universe was created</note></term> from Himself, He implanted within it, by His own will, an active essence which we call a spirit. Now, from the beginning, this spirit has been a restless, never-stationary essence; rather, from time to time it is incessantly mobile, active, and working without any cessation. # Acid, and how an Alkali is formed from that Acid.

Acidity presents itself, which we call by the common term an Acid <note>original: "Acidum"</note>. Now, the sharper the spirit becomes, the more earth it creates; for the acid causes a precipitation <note>the process of a solid settling out of a liquid solution</note>, and through this reveals a separation of the earths which were dissolved in the water, made thin and subtle, and turned into water; these the acid now reveals, and the more sour and heated this spirit becomes, the more it separates the earths.

However, so that such earth does not become too strong, and so that the acid does not "eat itself to death" <note>become neutralized or exhausted</note> upon it and become alkalized, the acid takes its nourishment from the Volatile <note>original: "à Volatili"; referring to substances that easily evaporate or the "spirituous" part of a compound</note>; it attracts this like a magnet, converts it into its own nature, and turns it into an acid. Now, the more the acid attracts the Volatile, the more it heats itself, and the more it ferments, the more it dissolves the earth—in which it must subsequently act again—and the more earth it dissolves, the more the acid is alkalized and fixed <note>original: "figirt"; rendered non-volatile or solid</note>. 

When the earth is fully impregnated with the acid, and the acid has dissolved as much earth as it was able to do, and has magnetically attracted as much of the Volatile as was necessary for its action, then the acid is no longer so strong for acting and precipitating. Instead, it stands in the middle, saturated by the earth (as the alkaline part) as well as by the Volatile; it now stands in the balance, waiting to see which of the two parts will gain the upper hand; it joins itself to that part immediately <note>original: "in continenti"</note> and helps it throughout to give birth to its own kind.

# How an Acid becomes an Alkali

# Part 1, Chapter 19: How from the Volatile a...

The most necessary and unavoidable axiom <note>A self-evident truth or principle.</note> based on reasons <note>original: "rationibus"</note> is the very common saying: **One cannot pass from one extreme to another without a middle ground.** <note>original: "Non transiri posse ab uno extremo ad alterum sine medio." This refers to the alchemical necessity of a "medium" or "bridge" to join opposing substances like fire and water.</note>

It would be too extensive for me to explain this more broadly <note>original: "fusius"</note> here; however, an artist <note>term: Artist (a practitioner of the alchemical arts)</note> is better served by physical reasons and authentic practice <note>original: "Praxi"</note> than if one proposes to him innumerable empty, ambiguous, and hieroglyphic speculations. For from a single, properly grasped reason and practice, he creates for himself a thousand other arguments that were never considered before; many other lights of the mind are ignited from a single light, whereby he is led ever closer to the target of truth <note>original: "scopum veritatis"</note>.

Many books of processes <note>term: Process-Bücher (laboratory manuals containing specific recipes)</note> are written, as well as other theories, but none or very few have been published which indicate for what reason this or that is added in this or that process, what fixes a substance there and what makes it volatile, what is the coagulant <note>original: "coagulans"</note> or the solvent <note>original: "solvens"</note>, and why or by what virtue such a thing happens. When an innocent beginner <note>term: Tyro (a novice or student)</note> stumbles upon such processes, he enters into them blindly until he sees the great error at the end. But if the learned world illustrated their books with true reasons that are also consistent with practice and true—even in such humble matters as they may be—then in a short time one would have to look with astonishment at a "wonder-birth" of our youth, who would then not have so much trouble sowing further fields and bringing the Art to its highest peak.

Now to the proposition: one cannot pass from one extreme to another without a middle ground <note>original: "non transiri posse ab uno extremo ad aliud sine medio"</note>. # Acid, and how an Alkali is made from Acid.

If one wishes to have and make an acid <note>original: "Acidum"</note>, let him take the specific principles belonging to each individual substance, or in the absence of one or the other, use homogeneous materials. Place one part of pure alkali <note>original: "alcali purum"</note> into a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, and pour three parts of its own acid upon it. Distill slowly in ash or in a water bath <note>original: "B. M." or Balneum Mariae, a vessel of hot water used for gentle heating</note>. In this way, the acid passes over very weakly, like a watery vapor <note>original: "phlegma"</note>, even if it had been as sharp as nitric acid <note>original: "Aquafort"</note>; for the alkali has retained the sharpness within itself and fixed it. When you have done this, pour another three parts of its own acid upon it again and proceed as before; it will once more pass over weakly, and the alkali will already be quite full and saturated. For the third time, pour fresh acid, three parts as before, over it—and the more, the better <note>original: "quo plus, eo melius"</note>. Draw it off in the water bath by degrees until it reaches the consistency of an oil; thus the alkali stands dissolved, and is the "full, wobbling peasant" <note>a metaphorical laboratory term for a saturated, heavy solution</note>. This pouring on of the acid is continued until the acid passes over just as sharp as it was when poured on. If the acid is sharp and concentrated, free of all watery phlegm, this often happens by the second, third, or fourth time. Now, when the acid is conjoined with the alkali and stands as an oil, the two principles are together. Here a chemist <note>original: "Chymist"</note> truly sees how one principle grasps and holds the other firmly and most sweetly <note>original: "suavissime"</note>, and it drives out its own heterogeneity itself—namely, the superfluous moisture or phlegm. Now, if you wish to make a rooted volatile <note>original: "Volatile radicatum"</note> from it, proceed as follows: for it is already a rooted acid <note>original: "Acidum radicatum"</note>, and there is nothing more to do than to add six parts of fresh vinegar <note>original: "Essig"</note> to it, and drive it over with that through a retort into a liquor by means of a few redistillations <note>original: "cohobia"</note>; thus it is a rooted vinegar or rooted acid <note>original: "Acetum vel Acidum radicatum"</note>.

# Chapter XX.

### What the Universal and Particular Volatile, Acid, and Alkali are.

In the preceding chapter, we discussed how an <term>Acid</term> <note>original: "Acidum"</note> is formed from the volatile, and from this an alkali is produced, *principally and generally* <note>original: "principaliter & generaliter"</note> from the regenerated chaos or rain-water, etc. But now we wish to explain what these substances actually are. The term "Volatile" is well-known for what it is: namely, a fleeting essence. We call it such because it is the most subtle and fleeting <term>Water</term> <note>original: "▽"</note> or essence in all things, as much in *universal* things as in *specific and individual* ones, because in a fiery **anatomy** <note>The author uses "anatomy" here to mean chemical analysis or distillation by fire.</note> it is obtained first, before its succeeding principles, whether it be thereafter in *liquid form* or *dry and coagulated*.

We call the Acid such because it comes after the volatile, and commonly brings a sour taste and smell to our tongue and nose. We have proven that in *universal subjects* this is Nitre <note>Saltpeter</note>, whether it be coagulated or made into a spirit: and this Acid is also otherwise called a "middle-thing," a hermaphrodite, or a middle nature between the volatile and the alkali—between the fleeting and the fixed. This is because this *part* or *principle* in *universal subjects* always follows after the volatile and <insert>before the alkali</insert>.

# Part 1, Chapter 23: What the Birth

The foundation, or the vessel of minerals, is that in which the fossils <note>In this period, "fossils" referred to anything dug out of the earth, including ores and stones.</note> are made; likewise, the vapor or Spirit of Salt <note>original: "Sp. That vitriol is formed first, before sulfur and arsenic, can be proven from the mineral-juice <note>original: "Gur"; a soft, earthy substance found in mines believed to be the "mother" of metals</note>; if one leaches, filters, and coagulates it, one finds a vitriolic salt according to the nature of the earth that dissolved it. But that metal is made from the marcasites through long fixation <note>original: "fixationem"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> is seen in that almost every marcasite yields a grain of perfect or imperfect metal in the assay.

# On the Nature of Minerals

It is more permanent: for the superfluous *recolaceum* moisture <note>original: "humidum recolaceum"; likely referring to a specific alchemical concept of "re-collecting" or "binding" moisture</note> is an instrument of the World-Spirit <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a vital force believed by alchemists to permeate all matter</note>. Everything there—stone, skin, and bone, whatever is in each mineral—is the World-Spirit or Spirit of Life, coagulated and fixed. # The First Chapter.

### In what manner Nature reduces the altered chaotic principles back to their first state, namely Saltpeter and Salt; that is, how she turns them back into vapor.

Just as we have demonstrated above how Nature gives birth to each and every thing from the ancient primordial—and then the re-generated—Chaos, rain or dew and snow-water, and how everything comes from these (whether it be still volatile, as it comes to us on Earth from the air, or already somewhat fixed and corporeal to the sight in the form of saltpeter and salt); so, on the contrary, by this very same Chaotic water, in both its volatile and fixed states, each and every thing is again destroyed, dissolved, resolved, and corrupted <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breaking down of a substance so it can be reborn into a new form.</note>, and brought back into its first essence from which it initially sprang: namely into saltpeter and salt, these into <term>Water</term> <note>Alchemy symbol for Water</note>, and the water into vapors. Nature creates her births by ascending <note>original: "ascendendo"</note> from the aforementioned principles up to their destined perfection; then she turns around and corrupts everything again by descending <note>original: "descendendo"</note> back to the very first beginning.

## The II. Chapter.
### In what manner Nature destroys the Animals.

Animals <note>original: "Animalia"</note> rot; they become maggots and worms, these become gnats, and these, after their appointed term, resolve themselves into the first essence of the universal border <note>original: "primum Ens limbi universalis," referring to the alchemical concept of the 'Limbus' or the primordial matter from which all things are organized</note>, that is, into a saline-nitrous or chaotic nature, then into water and steam, from which come dew and rain, and thus saltpeter <note>original: "Nitrum"</note> and a subtle, highly volatile salt are regenerated once again.

Animals are of a very moist and juicy nature and kind, full of volatile salt; therefore, as soon as their balsamic spirit of life <note>the "vital balsam" believed by Paracelsians to preserve the body from decay</note> has evaporated, they enter into putrefaction <note>decay</note>, begin to rot, swell up, and begin to stink. For the volatile element exhales and infects the air with a hideous stench; everything becomes slippery, damp, and wet. # How the Animal Kingdom is Destroyed

On the other hand, one can explain this better through the example of vegetables, because the process is almost identical. But whoever desires to have a better account of this, let him go to those areas where dead cattle lie—if it pleases him—and observe the changes daily; he will see more than he might like. Maggots crawl around in great numbers, not without a stench; these, once they are well-fattened, are transformed into gnats and flies. For if one simply takes well-fattened maggots, shuts them in a glass, and gives them a little stinking meat so that they have nourishment, and places it in lukewarm air—ensuring the glass is closed with a perforated paper—and if he places it in weak sunlight, he will see in a few short days and hours how the race of gnats or flies grows out of the maggots, and how they are transformed.

This comes in part from the volatile animal portion; the more fixed portion, however, which is not so fleeting and volatile <note>original: "volatilisch"</note>, becomes water and earth, from which a saltpeter and salt can be leached. These remaining parts, such as saltpeter and salt, are found in every subject <note>The "subject" refers to the specific matter being studied or decomposed</note> when it undergoes its ultimate reduction. The volatile part smokes [or: breathes out] and departs into the air in the form of vapor <note>original: "in forma vaporis"</note> to be "chaoticized" there <note>To be returned to the "Chaos," the primordial state of undifferentiated matter in the atmosphere</note>. The more fixed part, however, goes into the earth and water, to be reduced there into the first fixed seed <note>original: "primum fixius sperma"</note> of Gold <note>represented by the symbol ☉</note> and Salt <note>represented by the symbol ⊖</note>. From these reduced animal principles, vegetables grow once again; and thus the animal kingdom, by descending, becomes vegetable, as was taught in the first part.

# Part II, Chapter 4: How Nature [Produces] Minerals

In the whole world, everything and anything that is natural, visible and invisible, consists of all **Animals**, **Vegetables**, **Minerals**, and **Universals**. Or, the animals <note>original: "Animalia"</note> consume such vegetables as their food, and in this manner, the stone is transmuted for a second time: namely, into a vegetable, and from there into an animal. This animal rots and resolves itself into a chaotic-universal nature that is salty-nitrous, watery, vaporous, and primordial <note>original: "naturam chaotico-universalem salino-nitrosam, aquosam, vaporosam, hyleosam"</note>. Now the stone is once again the chaotic first matter <note>original: "materia prima chaotica"; the raw, unformed substance from which all things arise</note>.

Now you see how nature itself—slowly indeed, yet quite beautifully—retreats by degrees <note>original: "lente quidem... per gradus"</note>. Likewise, she also moves forward without great force, but rather lovely and without great noise; not with hammers and axes, or by hitting and pushing, but rather with and through fire and water she accomplishes everything. And if nature could have the salts as abundantly at hand as we do here in our art <note>original: "in arte nostra"; referring to the practice of alchemy</note>, she would operate as swiftly as we do. This can be seen on the highest mountains, where nature continually and daily tears away small stones, even large pieces, and sometimes sand and dust. The peasant takes better notice of this than a doctor sitting behind his stove, for such [operation and] generation of nature must be attributed to nature and to no one else. For no human, nor any four-footed animal with such a heavy body, ever climbs so high; and the weak birds would not be able to incessantly tear off stones weighing 10, 20, or 30 pounds and grind them to flour with their weak feet...

# Part II, Chapter 4: How Nature [Produces] Minerals

->**How Nature Transforms Minerals**<-

Here, a <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>A follower of Aristotle's philosophy, often used here to represent the traditional academic establishment of the 17th century.</note> would gladly like to see how I intend to prove to him that a cow should become a donkey, or an ox a human, and a human an ox, and a donkey a cow, etc. To assist him, and for the love and honor of the learned world and our Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or Hermetic chemistry.</note>, I must solve this knot. Now, if the donkey were to become a cow, it would be easily done if the cow took a donkey for food, or the donkey the cow. However, because the food of both the cow and the donkey are vegetables, we must first transform the donkey or the cow into a vegetable, and then give one to the other to eat. Let the donkey or the cow rot while dead under fresh earth, so that the earth is fertilized by them; from this, vegetables grow. Give these to one or the other to eat; thus the donkey, <term>having been made as a vegetable</term> <note>original Latin: "ut vegetabilis factus"</note>, will be changed into a cow within the cow's <term>archeus</term> <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, the "archeus" is the internal "alchemist" or vital force of an organ that directs digestion and growth.</note>; likewise, the cow becomes a donkey.

But as to how an ox becomes a human: we indeed eat beef daily and change it into our human substance, so that the entire ox puts aside its <term>bovine specification</term> <note>original Latin: "specificationem bovinam"; the specific essential traits that make it an ox.</note> within us, and is fully <term>transmuted into human substance</term> <note>original Latin: "substantiam humanam transmutirt"</note>, without <term>participating in the ox</term> <note>original Latin: "de bove participirend"</note> in the slightest trace. For if the ox remained an ox within us and did not put aside its form, then we humans would have to become nothing but oxen through the constant eating of beef. And so it goes with other <term>transmutations</term> <note>original Latin: "transmutationibus"</note> as well. If the human is also to become an ox, the human must rot in the earth and become a herb; if the ox eats this, then the human is <term>transmuted</term> into the ox.

Thus, such an "Orish" mercury <note>original: ☿</note>, arsenic, and marcasite can afterwards also be made into gold and silver through digestion and maturation, but not in the same way as metal is turned into pure gold and silver through casting and flux.

First, draw off the moisture gently, afterwards let it congeal ever more gently by degrees, and finally roast it a little more strongly than before; in this way, the earth attains a fixed color at the bottom, as can be seen when you take the flask out. When it is cold, take the flask out, grind the earth small again, and proceed as before in all things. It is one continuous operation, and the importance now lies in this: that the earth be roasted more strongly and again achieve a uniform color throughout...

# On the Regeneration of Chaotic Water into the Fifth Essence <note>original: "Regeneratione Chaoticæ Aquæ in Q. Ess." The Fifth Essence, or Quintessence, is the purest state of matter.</note>

That I do not, according to the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemists whose texts served as the foundation for this work.</note>, enclose the moisture <note>original: "humidum"</note> and the dryness <note>original: "siccum"</note> in a single vial, and through continuous digestion and circulation <note>original: "digestione & circulatione"; the process of heating a substance to circulate its vapors.</note> coagulate and fix it until it dries out and entirely becomes earth in a steady fire, etc.—Nature herself has taught me this. No Philosopher despises or thinks little of this; rather, whoever maintains the true natural path and purpose has won and has shortened his labor.

For Nature, in order that the elements of water and earth may bring forth their fruits, provides the seed from above in the form of water. The earth takes and retains as much of this as is necessary for its growth; the remaining superfluous water is driven back up into the air as vapor and smoke by both the lower and upper heat—that is, the subterranean central heat and the above-ground heat of the sun. There, it becomes water again and falls or distills back onto the earth. The earth once more takes as much as it needs for growth; the rest is distilled away again in the form of vapor, smoke, mist, etc., up into the air. 

Nature drives this circulation until the Creator's will coagulates and fixes everything together into a fixed stone. Under such soaking <note>original: "imbibition"</note> or distillation of the macrocosm <note>The "macrocosm" refers to the universe or the natural world as a whole, mirroring the "microcosm" of the alchemist's vessel.</note>, all fruits of the earth now grow, each according to its quality. For when the earth is dried out and reverberated <note>original: "reverberiret"; a process of intense heating or reflection of heat.</note> by the sun, the heavens give back moisture and soak it with rain and dew; then the sun comes again, dries it out <note>original: "exsicciret"</note>, coagulates, and reverberates the earth once more, so that it becomes thirsty to draw in moisture again.

# On the Regeneration of Chaotic Water into the Quintessential Essence

This treatise will surely provide some satisfaction, and as much as one might expect to find in others. And if one point or another should prove too difficult for the reader, let him run to Nature and speculate there; in that place, he has a wide field in which to pasture his thoughts.

To be sure, many cry out: "Follow Nature! Follow Nature!" Yes, but show me one who has ever truly investigated Nature to her very foundation. There are many hundreds, even thousands, of writers on nature <note>original: "Natur-Schreiber"</note> who wish to describe all things precisely. Indeed, it is true, they have done their part; but very many—in fact, most—have described only the shells and husks and not the kernel, only the exterior and not the innermost core. Through such writings, they have—albeit innocently and out of ignorance—ruined and misled many thousands of people who followed their dogmas <note>original: "Dogmatibus"</note>, explaining the author's intent <note>original: "mentem auctoris"</note> now one way, now another, arranging and believing it according to their own whims.

I confess that I am not capable of this. For who should venture to take upon themselves such an indescribable work of all things? But in this work, I show a philosopher <note>term: Philosopho (here referring to a practitioner of alchemy or natural philosophy)</note> as much as Nature permits, and I align all my works according to the works of Nature, so that a wanderer might be guided straight back—not here to me alone, but also to Nature and her works. Once he has grasped a handle on the matter, he may then direct his speculations <note>original: "speculationes"</note> further and form his arguments.

# On the Regeneration of Chaotic Water into the Quintessence

<note>original: "Regeneratione Chaoticæ Aquæ in Q. Ess."</note>

It is necessary for the incorruptible permanent moisture <note>original: "humido permanenti"; a term for the "fixed" liquid that does not evaporate in fire</note> to form and maintain itself. They hold this attracted moisture so firmly together with them that, in all fires, they flow steadily like wax without any smoke. This can be seen in flint and glass; once the superfluous moisture <note>original: "humidum superfluum"</note> has been driven out of them to the highest degree, they retain no more than what is necessary for them to flow like oil in the highest and strongest degree of fire, without any loss of stability or fixity <note>the state of being "fixed" or resistant to change by fire</note>, as long as they are not driven back again by nature or art.

For let a lover of this art <note>a "Liebhaber" or amateur/seeker of alchemy</note> only consider this: it would be an insurmountable task for an artist, as well as for Nature herself, if they were required to coagulate all the water or superfluous moisture—as much as each individual thing has concentrated within itself—into an earth, dry powder, or stone. Although it can be done, it happens too slowly and is entirely unnecessary for a philosopher <note>an alchemist</note>; one's greatest old age would prove too short for the task. Indeed, let someone just try it: seal rain or spring water in a vial and set it to coagulate; he will indeed find an earth, but in half a year or a whole year, he will perceive little or no decrease in the quantity of the water, nor will it have coagulated.

Therefore, we rightly follow Nature, which in the animal kingdom does not turn all moisture into the animal or an animal part; otherwise, animals would give off no urinary, sweaty, mucilaginous, or stercoral <note>fecal</note> excrements <note>original: "excrementa urinosa, sudorosa, mucilaginosa und stercorosa"</note>. # Part II, Chapter 5: On Separation and Conjunction

The beginning and foundation of all <term>coagulation</term> <note>the process of a liquid becoming solid or semi-solid</note> is this, and it is the closest thing in the Earth to being transformed into precious gemstones. Therefore, because such water is stripped of its saltiness, it cannot be coagulated or made earthy, or only does so very slowly. The Spirit, however, is of a salty and spermatic coagulating nature; no matter how volatile it may be, it can be coagulated far more easily than the <term>aqua recolacea</term> <note>literally "recollected water," likely referring to a distilled or residual moisture that lacks the "seed" of the metal</note>. However, if this water also becomes salty through <term>fermentation</term> <note>the process of ripening or transforming the substance through heat and additives</note>, then it can be coagulated just like the Seed and the Spirit. 

Because it does not allow itself to be coagulated, or does so incredibly slowly, we separate it by <term>distillando</term> <note>Latin: by distilling</note> to accelerate and shorten our work. We do this not because we discard it as useless, but because it hinders, retards, and delays us in the Work. For the Creator has created even the smallest grain of dust and the tiniest drop of water for His honor and glory and for the benefit of all His creatures. When we humans call such things "useless," it is to be understood only that it is superfluous and therefore unsuitable for us in this specific Work. The reader should grasp this <term>discours</term> <note>reasoning or explanation</note> well, for it contains not a single word in vain. If he does not understand it at once, let him speculate upon it until he does.

Now, one might also ask whether the *aqua recolacea* becomes the Seed, or the Seed becomes *aqua recolacea*. ## Part II, Chapter 5: On Separation and Conjunction <note>original: "De Separatione & Conjunctione"</note>

At a water-degree of heat, watery, easily-decaying cold fish and toad-like creatures are formed; in semi-dry and moist heat, nature creates more stable animals <note>original: "Animalia"</note>. Thus, in the air and in dry heat, she creates the vegetables <note>original: "Vegetabilia"</note>; and in even drier heat, the minerals <note>original: "Mineralia"</note>. For the perfect animals, she already makes use of a mild, dry heat, as they dwell upon and above the earth in the air. For the vegetables, however, she requires a stronger and drier heat, because they have harder and drier bodies than the animals. 

Furthermore, one sees that the sun constantly and strongly shines upon these plants along with the earth on which they grow; and because they cannot move away, they become very heated and dried out. In contrast, animals are mobile and can somewhat or entirely avoid such heat, seeking refuge in the cool or the shade.

If one were to set before a person a stone, or a mineral, or a corrosive and poison as his food, then everyone would immediately see that nature did not intend this as food for man; it is therefore contrary and heterogeneous <note>of a different kind or nature</note> to him. This is a dreg <note>original: "fex"</note> to the human being, for nature has not dedicated mineral subjects or poisons to man for food, but rather vegetables, such as bread and wine, etc., and animals, such as beef, veal, and mutton, etc. Such things are then homogeneous <note>of the same kind or nature</note> and pleasant to man. Therefore, every being takes its own kind into itself, and that which is contrary to it, it casts away as an excrement, dregs, or something heterogeneous. The secret lies within the coals and their <term>Sulfur</term><note>In alchemy, "Sulfur" refers to the combustible, oily, or soul-like principle of a substance, not just the chemical element S.</note>, once it has been resolved. The open jar will look white, while the covered one will look black. Boil the white mass into a lye, filter it, and coagulate it; then let it flow in a melting crucible. Afterward, take the black matter, pulverize it, and gradually add it into the salt of tartar <note>original: "Sal Tartari"</note> until it flows very thick and black-blue. Then quickly pour it out into a brass mortar, quickly pound it into a powder, put it into a flask, and pour spirit of wine <note>original: "Spir. vini," high-proof alcohol</note>—the kind that can ignite gunpowder—over it. Let it stand in gentle heat day and night, and it will extract the tincture. Pour this gently off from the residue, and you have the true tincture of the salt of tartar.

Likewise, take an animal or vegetable substance, as much as you wish, divide it as before, and burn it together in the furnace—one covered, the other not—so they are burned at the same time. Then leach the one into a lye, let it melt, and add the coal-black mass until it is saturated with color. Afterward, extract the tincture with spirit of wine or its own volatile spirit, and you have the true tincture of that individual substance.

### Third Way
->*The shortest path of separation in itself.*<- <note>original: "Via secum separatoria brevissima."</note>

Take the putrefied rain-water and distill off the volatile spiritual part from a <term>bladder-shaped vessel</term> <note>original: "vesica," a large copper distilling vessel</note>; set this aside specifically and mark it with **A**. Then distill off the phlegmatic <note>watery or dull</note> part until it reaches the thickness of thin, melted honey; keep this phlegm also separate and mark it with **B**. Take the honey-thick substance out of the vessel, place it in a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck</note>, set it in a sand bath, and distill first a coarser phlegm, then an <term>acid</term> <note>represented by the symbol ☩</note>, and afterwards, by increasing the heat in stages, the oil. # Of Animals

Since we now intend to describe a proper anatomy of things <note>original: "Anatomiam rerum"; here meaning the chemical deconstruction of matter</note>, we rightly begin to proceed according to the laws of nature <note>original: "legibus naturæ"</note>. We perfect this work according to her degrees of preparation, of putrefaction or solution, of distillation and rectification, of conjunction or coupling, and of coagulation and fixation. Just as all subjects and individuals in the entire wide world are distinguished one from another, so it is here also in the animal kingdom <note>original: "animalischen Reich"</note>. There are whole bodies with blood, flesh, veins, marrow, bone and skin, urine and dung, all of which are taken together for medicine. Conversely, one may take the separated parts of a body alone for medicine, such as the blood specifically, or the urine, dung, bones, skin, hair, horn, etc., and make a medicine from each part individually.

These pieces, both together and individually, we wish to describe: how to take them apart and join them together again, and how to bring them into a Quintessence <note>The "fifth essence," a highly purified and potent form of a substance</note>—first everything that is liquid, then the dry materials.

Above all others, this kingdom has the most loathsome and horrifying practice because of its stench during putrefaction <note>The process of allowing organic matter to rot to break it down chemically</note>. However, it possesses a more potent and rapid power to act because of its most penetrating volatile salt <note>original: "Salis volatilis"</note>, which the other kingdoms <note>The mineral and vegetable kingdoms</note> never have.

But I advise a chemist <note>original: "Chymisten"</note> not to work with blood while it is still warm directly from the animal. For it happened to me that as I wished to distill the more fixed parts via a retort <note>A glass vessel with a long neck used for distillation</note>, the *Evestrum* <note>A Paracelsian term referring to a ghostly double or an astral spirit associated with a physical body</note> appeared very monstrously in the receiver, from humans as well as other animals. Note: The volatile spirit and the coals are the two extremes; these will never unite without their middle nature. Their middle nature, however, is their water or phlegm <note>the watery, tasteless distillate</note>, their penetrating spirit or acid, and the oil. And these, again, do not unite if they are taken in reverse order, or at least so slowly that the effort and labor will vex you. For instance, if you wanted to join the volatile spirit and the oil, or the vinegar <note>acid</note> and the coals, and in the first case overwhelm it with vinegar and in the other with oil, it will not work. Therefore, one must maintain this order: just as one part came before the other during separation, so must they follow one another in the same order during conjunction. Then they will coagulate together immediately through moderate and proper degrees of fire <note>original: "gradus ignis"</note>.

Therefore, he who wishes to work faster, let him take the volatile with the phlegm (or separate the phlegm from it) and pour it to the acid (the Universal Solvent or Azoth <note>original: "Azoth," a term for the essential agent of transformation</note>).

Here I wish to make known two more ways: one entirely natural, just as nature itself operates, and the other artificial. # Of Minerals.

In order that they may become homogeneous with the previous kingdoms, the chemists <term>sweeten</term> <note>original: "dulcificiren"; the process of removing corrosive acidity or toxicity from a substance</note> minerals through and with vegetable and animal substances. Once they are sweetened, they are no longer mineral, but rather transmuted into a vegetable nature. When this vegetable substance is then consumed by an animal, or by a growing plant, it is transferred into the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: "ventriculo"</note> or the <term>digestive vessel</term> <note>original: "digestorio"</note>, and is transplanted and transmuted by its own <term>Archaeus</term> <note>The internal "alchemist" or vital force that Paracelsians believed governed the body's functions</note> into vegetable and animal matter. Thus, once sweetened, they are then homogeneous.

Therefore, for better understanding, we wish to set down here a **Tree of Sweetening and Harmony**, through which the animal is to be joined to the vegetable, and this or both to the mineral. By this means, sweetening comes to our hands, and the mineral can be consumed entirely without harm.

# Part II, Chapter 10: The Tree of Dulcification <note>Dulcification refers to the process of "sweetening" or neutralizing harsh, corrosive acids to make them medicinal.</note>

It follows now that I leave the universal seed or spirit—the Spirit of Niter <note>Nitric acid</note> or *Aqua Fortis* <note>literally "strong water," a powerful corrosive acid</note> etc.—as the solvent with the solute <note>the dissolved substance</note>; and I provide this reasoning: When the universal seed or spirit is joined to the specified seed, and thus the universal spirit becomes a specific thing itself through that which is specified, then the mother indeed comes to the child, or the child to the mother. The mother nourishes and increases the child with her own food; likewise, the child draws its nourishment from the mother, from whose substance and blood it initially sprouted. Therefore, I do not know what harm could come if the child is fed by its rightful mother, and transforms such food into its own quality and nature, by which it is different from the mother; nor will it be harmful if the child has taken and promoted its growth thereby.

All universals <note>substances acting on a general or cosmic level</note> indeed make themselves homogenous to the specifics, taking on their nature and quality, and carry out the predestined power of the specific. Thus, not only is the virtue and power increased by the concentrated and therefore sharpened universal seed, but it is also extended and elevated in quantity and quality. And the sharper and more fiery the spirit is, the more and more powerfully it works; the more concentrated it is, the stronger it is, and the smaller its dose.

Thus, I have also not taught to apply such a sharp spirit to vegetables and animals before its dulcification; however, after the dulcification, let someone prove a fault. Whoever will not believe it theoretically, practice <note>original: "praxis"</note> will surely teach them, and set it before their face <note>original: "illi ad faciem," meaning to prove it to them directly</note>.

# The Mineral Secret
<note>original: "Arcanum Minerale"</note>

It is known to all practitioners <note>literally "Artists," referring to alchemists or chemical philosophers</note> that it possesses this quality; however, the fact that it is more sulfurous than mercurial is no hindrance. It was proven above that mercury <note>symbol: ☿</note> and all arsenical-mercurial subjects are derived from sulfur. All this hesitation and over-analysis is of no consequence, provided that it produces its intended effect. Furthermore, how many authors are there who establish that vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfate</note> is the first matter of metals <note>original: "primam materiam metallorum"</note> just as much as mercury? They have even recommended it as the material for the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>, as that saying goes: *By visiting the interior of the earth, etc.* <note>original: "Visitando interiora terræ," a reference to the alchemical acronym V.I.T.R.I.O.L.: Visita Interiora Terrae Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem</note>. If vitriol is indeed the first matter of metals, then it must certainly have the power to reduce metals back to their first state after their resolution, and it must also be homogenous to all minerals. If it is the material of the Stone, then it is indeed the extract or the "fifth essence" <term>quintessence: the purest and most concentrated essence of a substance</term> of the entire mineral kingdom.

Now, it is also well known that saltpeter and salt are a universal subject, which many also recommend as the physical subject found in every manure pile. They call it "all in all" because it is found everywhere; and because it is universal, it is an indifferent subject <note>a neutral base</note> capable of receiving every form or specification. Within the vitriol, they become specified and become one with it; they remain both volatile and fixed alongside it. Whatever they dissolve, they make volatile again and then fixed again, remaining with them inseparably. Whoever thinks to separate them merely separates the volatile part, while the fixed part remains nonetheless: for one seed gladly remains with another—especially the specific and the universal—and they let the residual water <note>original: "aqua recolacea"</note> depart from them.

Therefore, it is a folly of many erring laboratory workers <note>original: "Laboranten"</note> who think they are separating the solvents <note>original: "menstrua"</note>

# Chapter XI & Last.
## Concerning the Alkahest or Alka est.

In order that the reader may have a true understanding of the much-celebrated *Alkahest circulati* <term>mercurial</term> <note>original: "☿"</note> *acerrimi* <note>Latin: "the sharpest or most potent circular mercury"</note>, I wish to report on it descriptively, and with this, bring this book to a close.

So that I do not commit too great a long-windedness: the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to historical alchemists like Paracelsus or Helmont</note>, after they saw that they could accomplish little or nothing through common corrosives according to the aforementioned understanding, discovered and struck upon a remedy. For when a corrosive dissolves an acidic metal, it does not dissolve an alkaline one; and whichever corrosive dissolves alkaline subjects does not dissolve acidic ones. This is because the <term>acidum</term> <note>acid</note> and <term>alcali</term> <note>alkali</note>, when they come together, devour one another unto death and give birth to a <term>tertium</term> <note>a third, neutral substance</note>. Therefore, they looked about in Nature to see if a subject could be found which would dissolve both acidic and alkaline subjects without distinction—one just like the other—and perform the same action in the solution. After they had searched through everything, they all saw that it must be a hermaphroditic subject <note>A substance containing both "male/active" and "female/passive" principles</note> that embraced both natures and associated itself with both this one and that one. Such a thing they found, among others, in all mercurial subjects, such as all <term>arsenicalia</term> <note>arsenic-based minerals</note>, <term>marcasitæ</term> <note>marcasites or iron pyrites</note>, and <term>realgaria</term> <note>realgar, a red arsenic sulfide</note> after the <term>sulphur combustibile</term> <note>combustible sulfur</note> has been separated; and in all <term>Mercuriis currentibus & coagulatis</term> <note>Latin: "mercuries, both flowing (liquid) and coagulated (solid)"</note>. They took such Mercuries and again made a selection among them, according to how each

# Part II, Chapter II: Concerning the Alkahest

To call for help, and whether willing or unwilling, to embrace <note>original: "amplectiren," alternatively "imploriren" (to implore)</note> the corrosive substances, without which the Mercury <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to the "spirit" or fluid principle of metals, not just the common liquid metal.</note> would not fight. Now, as one person had a better or worse way than another, they sharpened their Mercury through salts <note>original: "Salia"</note> as best they could. Some took animal, vegetable, and mineral salts mixed together to sharpen the Mercury; some took vegetable and animal; some universal and mineral, according to which path succeeded for them. They then recommended this path so zealously as if no other existed in Nature, and as if they alone were the ones who had overturned all of Nature. When they had then turned Mercury into salt, they likely thought: Nature, in all generation and corruption <note>The natural cycle of birth/growth and decay/death.</note>, used a water for every mixture, and made almost a dry compound <note>original: "compositum"</note> for which she necessarily required a water. Therefore, they turned this salty Mercury into a "water-water," so that by means of such extension it should better penetrate the metals and minerals, and reach into the very center of the soul <note>original: "centrum animæ"</note>; then they took such Mercury and turned it into a water beyond water. The more penetrating the water was, the better and faster the Mercury attacked the metals; however, the weaker the water, the slower their Mercury began to dissolve.
